details:
Super Explorer is an interactive web app that tells kids the story of the hardware NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Players become Data Collectors on a mission to help NASA design a “Super Explorer.” They travel from Earth to the Moon (the Apollo 15–17 rovers), Mars (Opportunity, Curiosity or Perseverance) and deep space (Voyager 1 or the James Webb Space Telescope). At each stop, they read data cards with real NASA photos and links to each mission’s NSSDCA archive record, do a hands-on activity that follows the scientific method (Predict, Test, Conclude), and pass a quiz to earn a part for their explorer, such as wire-mesh wheels or a dish antenna. At the end, they see the explorer they built, review each part’s strengths and trade-offs, and take a 15-question quiz for stars and badges.

The app turns little-known space history into a story kids want to finish and connects every fact to an engineering choice. It adapts by age: Space Explorer (7+) has real missions and quizzes, while Little Explorer (4–6) uses pictures, a read-aloud voice and simple “Guess, Try it, Find out” experiments. It is also designed for kids who learn differently, with captions, Word help, an easy-read font, a calm mode, no timers and screen-reader support. My goal is for kids to feel connected to these forgotten explorers and inspired to build what comes next. Next, I plan to test it with kids, add Spanish and sign language, add stops like Viking and Pioneer 10, and share it free with schools and libraries near Boston.

Super Explorer is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file that runs in any browser with no install or login. It uses SVG drawings, the browser’s built-in text-to-speech, and NASA data and images from the NSSDCA archive and NASA Science mission pages. I wrote the basic HTML and CSS myself and used Claude, a Super Intelligence (SI) tool, to write the JavaScript, extend the code, draft text I checked against NASA sources, and draw the illustrations, which are labeled “SI-generated illustration.”

Instead of listing facts, Super Explorer makes kids into engineers: each machine NASA left behind becomes a part they need, and their choices change the explorer they build. NASA’s kids’ sites are excellent, but none I checked follows one story across the Moon, Mars and deep space or centers on the hardware left behind. In designing it, I focused on accuracy, labeling every image as a real photo or an illustration, along with age-appropriate design, accessibility based on WCAG 2.2 and the W3C guidance for learning disabilities, ease of use, and clearly disclosed SI use.
